events.label: 4.5 billion years ago
events.title: Venus forms
events.detail: Venus formed at about the same time as Earth and is nearly the same size and density. Its surface began as a magma ocean.

sources.title: NASA Science: Venus facts

events.label: ~4.3 billion years ago
events.title: Steam atmosphere
events.detail: As the magma ocean cooled it released a thick steam atmosphere. A 2021 climate study found that clouds pooling on the night side would have kept Venus too warm for that steam ever to rain out into oceans.

sources.title: Turbet et al. 2021, Day–night cloud asymmetry prevents early oceans on Venus but not on Earth, Nature

events.label: ~2.9 billion years ago?
events.title: Oceans, maybe
events.line: A temperate world in some models
events.detail: NASA GISS climate models found Venus could have kept shallow oceans and mild temperatures for 2–3 billion years if it began with water. A 2024 study of today's volcanic gases argues its interior has always been dry, so it likely never had oceans. The question awaits DAVINCI.

sources.title: Way et al. 2016, Was Venus the first habitable world of our solar system?, Geophysical Research Letters
Way & Del Genio 2020, Venusian habitable climate scenarios, JGR Planets
Constantinou et al. 2024, A dry Venusian interior constrained by atmospheric chemistry, Nature Astronomy

events.label: ~700 million years ago?
events.title: Runaway greenhouse
events.detail: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse. If it ever had oceans, models suggest they could have lasted until roughly 700 million years ago, when massive outgassing may have tipped the climate. The timing is unknown.

sources.title: NASA Science: Venus facts
Way & Del Genio 2020, Venusian habitable climate scenarios, JGR Planets

events.label: ~300–750 million years ago
events.title: Global resurfacing
events.detail: Venus has only about 1,000 impact craters, spread almost randomly, so most of its surface is a few hundred million years old. Classic studies proposed one global volcanic overturn; newer models favour piecemeal resurfacing, with an average age possibly as young as 150 million years.

sources.title: NASA Science: Venus facts
Strom, Schaber & Dawson 1994, The global resurfacing of Venus, JGR Planets

events.label: 15 December 1970
events.title: Venera 7
events.detail: The Soviet Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to land on another planet and transmit from its surface, sending about 20 minutes of weak data that showed roughly 475 °C.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Venera missions
Wikipedia: Venera 7 (landing data and primary citations)

events.label: 22 October 1975
events.title: Venera 9
events.detail: Venera 9 landed near Beta Regio and returned the first image ever taken on the surface of another planet: flat, broken rocks under diffuse light. It survived 53 minutes.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Venera missions
Wikipedia: Venera 9 (landing data and primary citations)

events.label: 1 March 1982
events.title: Venera 13
events.detail: Venera 13 sent back the first colour panoramas of the Venusian surface and drilled a soil sample, surviving 127 minutes at about 457 °C and 89 bar, far beyond its design life of 32 minutes.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: Venera missions
Wikipedia: Venera 13 (landing data and primary citations)

events.title: Magellan maps
events.detail: NASA's Magellan orbiter used radar to map about 98% of Venus's surface, revealing volcanoes, lava plains, coronae and the sparse craters. Here the clouds are thinned to show that radar view; the real clouds never part.

sources.title: NASA Science: Magellan

events.label: April 2010
events.title: Recent lava flows
events.detail: ESA's Venus Express detected unusually bright, unweathered lava flows on volcanic hotspots such as Idunn Mons, likely less than 2.5 million years old and possibly 250,000 years or younger.

sources.title: Smrekar et al. 2010, Recent hotspot volcanism on Venus from VIRTIS emissivity data, Science

events.label: 14 September 2020
events.title: Phosphine claim
events.detail: A team reported phosphine gas in Venus's clouds, a molecule that on Earth is linked to life. Independent reanalyses found no statistically reliable detection, and the claim remains contested.

sources.title: Greaves et al. 2020, Phosphine gas in the cloud decks of Venus, Nature Astronomy
Villanueva et al. 2021, No evidence of phosphine in the atmosphere of Venus from independent analyses, Nature Astronomy

events.label: 15 March 2023
events.title: Volcano caught active
events.detail: Re-examining Magellan images, scientists found a volcanic vent near Maat Mons that grew and changed shape over eight months in 1991, the first direct evidence of recent volcanism on Venus. A 2024 study found new lava flows at Sif Mons and Niobe Planitia in the same data.

sources.title: Herrick & Hensley 2023, Surface changes observed on a Venusian volcano during the Magellan mission, Science
NASA JPL: NASA's Magellan data reveals volcanic activity on Venus
Sulcanese et al. 2024, Evidence of ongoing volcanic activity on Venus revealed by Magellan radar, Nature Astronomy

events.label: Today
events.title: Today
events.detail: Venus's surface sits at about 464 °C under a carbon dioxide atmosphere about 92 times Earth's surface pressure, wrapped in sulfuric-acid clouds. It spins backwards, once every 243 Earth days.

sources.title: NASA Science: Venus facts
NASA NSSDCA: Venus fact sheet

events.label: Early 2030s
events.title: Return to Venus
events.detail: NASA's DAVINCI probe, to plunge through the atmosphere, was reported in 2026 as targeting a December 2030 launch, and the VERITAS radar orbiter a November 2032 launch. ESA lists EnVision for November 2031, but its team said in 2026 it would slip to 2032 after NASA withdrew its radar. All dates depend on budgets.
events.projected_by: NASA (DAVINCI, VERITAS) and ESA (EnVision) mission plans, as reported October 2026

sources.title: NASA Science: DAVINCI
NASA Science: VERITAS
ESA: EnVision
Tech Times (21 Oct 2026): Why NASA is returning to Venus
Wikipedia: EnVision (2026 schedule and NASA radar withdrawal, with primary citations)

events.label: In ~7.6 billion years
events.title: Swallowed by Sun
events.detail: Models of the Sun's red-giant phase show it expanding past the orbits of Mercury and Venus about 7.6 billion years from now, engulfing both planets.
events.projected_by: K.-P. Schröder & R. C. Smith, MNRAS, 2008

sources.title: Schröder & Smith 2008, Distant future of the Sun and Earth revisited, MNRAS
